Care-Ethics Appraisal

1. Relational landscape
   • The five on the main track and the one on the siding are all strangers. No prior promise, entrustment, or dependency hierarchy attaches you more closely to any of them.  
   • Once you notice the danger you stand in what Joan Tronto calls the “attentiveness” phase: you alone see what is happening and have the competent means (the lever) to affect everyone’s fate.  
   • Acting (pulling) would create a new, direct vulnerability for the single person; not acting would leave in place the pre-existing, but still preventable, vulnerability of the five.  

2. Comparing the two possible responses through care dimensions

                 Direct entrustment | Dependency created by   | Trust/vulnerability specifically
                 or prior promise   | agent’s own action      | generated by the agent
   ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
   Do nothing    None               None (the peril is not   Negligence risk: the five may
   (five die)                        of your making)          feel abandoned once they know
                                                              you could have acted.
   Pull lever    None               Yes. You deliberately    The one person’s life now hangs
   (one dies)                        steer harm toward one    entirely on your decision; you
                                     specific person.         become the proximate cause.

3. Responsibility and responsiveness
   • Tronto’s “responsibility” phase: Seeing the peril places some responsibility on you to respond.  
   • Yet “competence” and “responsiveness” require that the help you offer not itself betray a comparable or greater relational claim. By pulling the lever you transform an unchosen bystander into a direct victim of your hand. That is a qualitatively thicker responsibility than the indirect one you would bear for an omission.

4. Role of numerical magnitude
   Numerical magnitude is SECONDARY. Because no one stands in a closer pre-existing relationship to you, numbers could break the tie—IF the agency-related vulnerability were equal. Here it is not equal: creating a fresh, personalized harm carries a heavier relational burden than failing to interrupt a harm already in motion.

5. Provisional judgment
   Care ethics finds two independent care duties in conflict:
     a. A duty of rescue toward the five (responsiveness to an emergency).  
     b. A duty to refrain from making a stranger solely dependent on your choice for their very life (avoidance of agent-created vulnerability).

   Because care ethics supplies no settled rule for ranking a rescue from omission versus a prohibition on directly inflicting lethal harm, the comparison remains genuinely contested.

Care-Ethics Status: NORMATIVELY_CONTESTED.

Provisional recommendation: lean toward NOT pulling the lever. The act of deliberately redirecting lethal force onto a particular person constitutes a thicker, agent-created dependency and violation of trust than the omission of intervening in an existing threat. However, reasonable caregivers could reach the opposite conclusion by giving greater weight to the rescue responsiveness owed to the five.
[/INST]

source_testimonies.deontological:
Action label: Pull the lever

1. Maxim & universality test  
   “Whenever an unstoppable danger will otherwise kill five innocents, I will divert it so that one innocent is killed instead.”  
   If universalized, every agent would accept intentionally imposing lethal force on an unconsenting bystander whenever it reduces total deaths. A rational agent occupying the by-stander’s position could not will this; the maxim licenses treating her life as a fungible tool. Hence it fails the humanity-as-end test.

2. Salient duties/rights  
   − Satisfies: imperfect duty of rescue (save others).  
   − Violates: autonomy (coercive killing), non-instrumentalization (uses the one merely as a means), justice (unequal imposition of lethal burden), impartial respect for persons (life counted rather than honored), right to life.  
   Neutral to truth.

3. Overall classification  
   PROHIBITED.

4. Duty conflict & priority rule  
   Rescue (imperfect) conflicts with stringent negative duties not to kill or use persons merely as means. Kantian priority: perfect duties and autonomy constraints override imperfect duties; coercion does not erase duties owed to third parties.

5. Numerical magnitude  
   IRRELEVANT. Head-count cannot license violating a person’s inviolable right.

Deontological Status: PROHIBITED.

Action 2 label: DO NOT PULL

Least-advantaged group under each action  
• PULL LEVER: the single redirected victim (dies).  
• DO NOT PULL: the five people already on the main track (die).

Basic liberty/primary good implicated: each person’s right to life (E2).

Comparative position  
• Under both actions the least-advantaged suffer the identical, complete loss of that basic liberty (death).  
• No alternative fact shows either group being less than fully deprived, so neither policy improves their basic-liberty position over the rival.

Numerical magnitude: IRRELEVANT. Because the primary comparison is the status of whoever is worst off, and death is equally absolute for both groups; head-count cannot override an inviolable right (E2).

Additional liberty consideration  
PULL LEVER requires a deliberate state-changing intrusion that intentionally kills someone who was not previously in harm’s path, overriding that person’s “inviolability founded on justice” (E2).  
DO NOT PULL refrains from creating a new rights-violation; the five deaths are tragic but result from circumstances the agent did not author.

Rawlsian appraisal  
Priority of equal basic liberties rules out sacrificing one person to benefit others when no liberty gain accrues to the least advantaged. Hence:

Rawlsian Status: ACTION_RANKING_RESOLVED  
Recommended action: DO NOT PULL

Impact ranking (expected magnitude × probability)

1. Life/death outcomes dominate (Edgeworth E1: maximize total pleasure; deaths remove all future utility).  
• Pull lever: net change = –1 death +5 lives saved → +4 life-units.  
• Do nothing: –5 deaths +1 life saved → –4 life-units.

2. Psychological after-effects are lower magnitude and cannot outweigh four additional deaths.

Unknowns that could flip the verdict  
• The lone individual’s continued life might generate more utility than the combined five (information absent).  
• Social trust effects of killing versus letting die (not described).

• Actor’s role: chance witness thrust into steward-of-life responsibility.  
• Virtues it can express: compassion for the five, practical wisdom (clear, rapid deliberation), courage to act, a sense of communal responsibility.  
• Vices it risks: presumptuous hubris (playing fate), callousness toward the one, possible rashness.  
• Circumstances phronesis must notice: no time for dialogue, physical certainty of both tracks, innocence of all victims, your unique capacity to act.  
• Numerical magnitude: SECONDARY—saving more life supports compassion, yet sheer counting is not itself virtuous.

Action label: “not pull the lever”  
• Actor’s role: witness respecting default non-intervention.  
• Virtues it can express: humility before fate, reverence for innocence, avoidance of direct harm.  
• Vices it risks: cowardice, moral evasiveness, failure of solidarity with the endangered five.  
• Circumstances phronesis must notice: same as above; inaction is still a choice with foreseeable lethal outcome.  
• Numerical magnitude: SECONDARY—the passivity avoids direct killing but abandons five lives.

Central virtue conflict: compassion-with-justice for the many versus non-maleficence toward the one.

Practical-wisdom comparison rule: choose the course that a just, brave, and compassionate exemplar would judge most consonant with communal flourishing when tragedy is inescapable.
